title: Hinduism, a Family of Traditions
objective: After this level you can explain why Hinduism has no single founder, creed or central authority, and where the word "Hindu" comes from.
summary: Hinduism has no single founder, scripture or agreed set of teachings, so it is often called a family of religions. Its name comes from Sindhu, the river Indus.

cards.headline: No single founder, no single holy book, no agreed creed. Is it one religion?
cards.body: About 15 percent of the world's people were Hindu in 2020. Yet Hinduism has no founder to point to and no single book everyone must accept. Many writers answer the puzzle by calling it a family. Let's see why, starting with its name.

cards.headline: A family, not a single church
cards.body: Hinduism has no single founder, no single scripture and no commonly agreed set of teachings. Over its long history, many teachers taught different philosophies and wrote many holy books. That's why writers often call it "a way of life" or "a family of religions" rather than one religion. Think of a big family reunion: nobody at the party started the family, yet everyone knows they belong.

cards.headline: A name borrowed from a river
cards.body: The word Hindu comes from Sindhu, the Sanskrit name for the river Indus. Persians, and later Greeks, used the river's name for the land and the people who lived there. So the name began as geography, not theology. The "ism" came much later: British writers coined "Hinduism" in the early 19th century. Many Hindus prefer their own name for their tradition, sanatana dharma, "the eternal law".

cards.headline: What the family shares
cards.body: Hard to define doesn't mean shapeless. Hinduism is rooted in India, which in 2020 was home to 95 percent of the world's Hindus. Most Hindus revere a body of scripture called the Veda. Most draw on a shared set of values called dharma: duty, virtue, the right way to live. Like any family, its members share a home, a library and a way of life, even when their customs differ.

cards.headline: Hinduism, a Family of Traditions: the takeaways
learned: Hinduism has no single founder, scripture or creed
"Hindu" comes from Sindhu, the river Indus
Most Hindus share the Veda and dharma

questions.prompt: Where does the word "Hindu" come from?

options.label: The Sanskrit name of the river Indus
The title of its oldest holy book
options.rationale: The oldest scripture is the Veda.

options.label: A word coined by a medieval king
options.rationale: It began as the name of a river.

questions.explanation: Hindu comes from Sindhu, the river Indus; Persians and Greeks used the river's name for the land and its people.

questions.prompt: Why do writers often call Hinduism "a family of religions"?

options.label: All Hindus descend from a single family line
It was founded by a family of priests
It has no single founder, scripture or agreed set of teachings
It was formed by merging foreign faiths
options.rationale: Its variety grew over its own long history.

questions.explanation: With no single founder, scripture or agreed set of teachings, and many teachers and holy books, Hinduism is often called a family of religions.

questions.prompt: Level 4 said every tradition is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions. How does Hinduism fit that idea?

options.label: It is the one exception, with one unified teaching
options.rationale: It has no commonly agreed set of teachings.

options.label: It fits only because of its Persian-given name
options.rationale: The name came from a river; the variety is the point.

options.label: It doesn't fit, because it has a single founder
It is a clear case, with many teachers, philosophies and holy books

questions.explanation: Smart's idea fits Hinduism well: many teachers, different philosophies and many holy books, held together as a family.
